title: Boethius in prison
hookLine: condemned and waiting, he writes the Consolation of Philosophy, where Lady Philosophy comes to his cell

lines: A WOMAN IN A TORN ROBE.
cards: A man sits in confinement, writing sad poems. Not long ago he was a powerful official at the king's court. Now, as he tells it in his own book, he's condemned, his good name gone, and he's waiting.
The Muses of poetry stand around his bed, feeding him lines of grief. Then a woman appears above his head, her robe old and torn, as if rough hands had ripped pieces away.
She sends the Muses packing, sits on the edge of his bed, and wipes his eyes with a fold of her dress. He knows her. She's Philosophy.

teach.b: The book is the Consolation of Philosophy, a conversation between a broken man and the wisdom he had studied all his life. Philosophy doesn't start with comfort. She starts with diagnosis: you've forgotten who you are.
Then, in the second book, comes an image: Fortune's wheel. In one passage Philosophy speaks in Fortune's own voice. I turn a wheel, Fortune says.
I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unfair when it brings you down again; that's the game you agreed to play. Change isn't Fortune betraying you.
Change is what Fortune is. So Philosophy asks Boethius to look at what he's lost: money, office, applause. Were they ever really his?

teach.h: WHAT CAN BE TAKEN WAS ON LOAN.
teach.b: What can be taken away was only on loan.
What can't be taken is the good itself, and Philosophy leads him, step by step, toward God as that highest good, the still center the wheel turns around.
Boethius was a Christian who wrote on the Trinity, yet this book never names Christ. The help comes from reason. Christian readers have still treasured it, hearing echoes of scripture.

Hannah's song in First Samuel: "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up." And Job, stripped of everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

how: Christian readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss, and the image of Fortune's wheel appears in Christian art, poetry and preaching.

o: a saint jailed for preaching about Christ
a condemned man consoled by Philosophy in his cell
a monk who chose a cell to pray alone

p: a woman in a torn robe
turns the wheel, low up, high down
the LORD gave, and hath taken away

s: Philosophy comforts Boethius by promising he'll get his old life back
she tells him his losses were only on loan, and turns him toward the good that can't be taken.
Boethius wrote on the Trinity elsewhere, but in this book the help comes from Philosophy.
in the book, Fortune's wheel turning is a betrayal
Fortune says change is simply what she is: climb on, and don't call it unfair when you come down.

games.q: you're Philosophy. you find your old student in a cell, writing sad poems with the Muses. what do you do first?
o: join in and help him write sadder poems.
send the Muses away and tell him he's forgotten who he is.
games.why: she drives off the Muses, wipes his eyes, and starts with a diagnosis: he has forgotten who he is.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that's gone badly lately, a loss, a no, a door that closed, and let it be as heavy as it is.
Picture a wise friend on the edge of your bed, the way Philosophy sat with Boethius, asking what this took that was only on loan, and what's still yours; if you pray, bring both answers to God.
If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Boethius in prison. A condemned man whose Consolation of Philosophy turns him from Fortune's wheel to the good that can't be taken.

orig.note: Latin: the wheel of Fortune, the image at the heart of book two of the Consolation.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel turns. The still center doesn't. I'll be here tomorrow.
